<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Over half of US adults with Alzheimer disease and related dementias (ADRD) remain undiagnosed. Speech-based screening algorithms offer a scalable approach, but the relative value of large language model (LLM) adaptation strategies is unclear.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study aimed to compare LLM adaptation strategies for cognitive impairment detection across DementiaBank speech datasets using both text-only and multimodal models.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We analyzed audio-recorded speech from 237 participants in the ADReSSo subset of DementiaBank (ADRD vs cognitive normal [CN]) and report performance on a held-out test set (n=71). Nine text-only LLMs (3B-405B; open-weight and commercial) and 3 multimodal audio-text models were evaluated. Adaptations included (1) in-context learning (ICL) with 4 demonstration selection strategies (most similar, least similar, average similar or prototype, and random), (2) reasoning-augmented prompting (self- or teacher-generated rationales, self-consistency, tree-of-thought with domain experts), (3) parameter-efficient fine-tuning (token-level vs added classification head), and (4) multimodal audio-text integration. Generalizability of the adaptation strategies was evaluated on the DementiaBank Delaware dataset (n=205; mild cognitive impairment vs CN) using the first 3 strategies. The primary outcome was the
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      -score for the cognitive impaired class; the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was reported when available.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      On the ADReSSo dataset, average similar (prototype) demonstrations achieved the highest ICL performance across model sizes (
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      -score up to 0.81). Reasoning primarily benefited smaller models: teacher-generated rationales increased LLaMA 8B from
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      -score 0.72 to 0.76; expert-role tree-of-thought improved its zero-shot score from 0.65 to 0.71. Token-level fine-tuning produced the highest scores (LLaMA 3B:
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      =0.83, 95% CI 0.01, area under the curve [AUC]=0.91; LLaMA 70B:
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      =0.82, 95% CI 0.02, AUC=0.86; GPT-4o:
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      =0.79, 95% CI 0.01, AUC=0.87). A classification head markedly improved MedAlpaca 7B (
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      =0.06, 95% CI 0.02 to
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      =0.81, 95% CI 0.04), indicating model-dependent benefits of this approach. Among multimodal models, fine-tuned Phi-4 Multimodal reached an
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      -score of 0.80 (cognitive impaired) and 0.75 (CN) but did not exceed the top text-only systems. On the Delaware dataset, ICL achieved a high performance (LLaMA 8B:
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      =0.74; GPT-4o:
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      =0.80). Reasoning-augmented ICL improved LLaMA 8B to an
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      -score of 0.75. Token-level fine-tuning produced the highest scores (LLaMA 8B:
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      =0.76, 95% CI 0.02; GPT-4o:
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      =0.82, 95% CI 0.03).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Detection accuracy is influenced by demonstration selection, reasoning design, and tuning method. Token-level fine-tuning is generally most effective, while a classification head benefits models that perform poorly under token-based supervision. Properly adapted open-weight models can match or exceed commercial LLMs, supporting their use in scalable speech-based ADRD and mild cognitive impairment screening. Current multimodal models may require improved audio-text alignment and/or larger training corpora.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Large Language Model Adaptation Strategies in Speech-Based Cognitive Screening: Systematic Evaluation
